blocks.text: **The problem.** `n` friends sit in a circle, numbered 1 to n clockwise. Starting at friend 1, count `k` friends clockwise, including the one you start on; the k-th friend **leaves** the circle. Counting starts again from the friend just after them. Repeat until one friend is left, and return their number. (This is the classic **Josephus problem**.)

blocks.alt: Five friends, 1 to 5, around a circle with k equal to 2. Counting two at a time, friend 2 leaves first, then 4, then 1, then 5. Friend 3 is the last one left and wins.

blocks.code:
n = 5, k = 2   ->  3     (2, 4, 1, 5 leave in that order)
n = 6, k = 5   ->  1
n = 4, k = 1   ->  4     (everyone leaves in order; the last one wins)

blocks.text: The idea: a circle of people is a circular linked list

The friends form a **ring**: after friend n comes friend 1 again, and when someone leaves, their two neighbours become neighbours. That is exactly a **circular linked list** — counting is following `next`, and leaving is unlinking one node, `prev.next = prev.next.next`. To unlink you need the node **before** the one leaving, so the walk keeps a pointer on the node before the current count.

Simulating is O(n · k). There's also a famous formula: if you know who wins with **i − 1** friends, the winner with **i** friends is that position shifted by k, wrapping round — which gives an O(n) loop with no list at all.
1. Simulate with a circular linked list

blocks.caption: Count k round the ring, unlink the k-th friend, and count on from the next one.

blocks.code:
def find_the_winner(n, k):
    head = ListNode(1)                   # friends 1..n sitting in a ring
    tail = head
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        tail.next = ListNode(i)
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = head
    prev = tail                          # the node before whoever counts "1"
    while prev.next is not prev:         # until one friend is left
        for _ in range(k - 1):           # count k - 1 friends
            prev = prev.next
        prev.next = prev.next.next       # the k-th friend leaves the circle
    return prev.val

blocks.text: **Time O(n · k), space O(n).** There are n − 1 rounds, each counting k − 1 steps, and removing a friend is one pointer change. The loop ends when the last node points to itself.
2. Simulate with an array and index arithmetic

Instead of walking k steps, compute the position directly: from the start index, the k-th friend is at `(start + k − 1) mod size`. Removing them from an array shifts everyone after them one place left, so the next round starts at the same index.

blocks.code:
def find_the_winner(n, k):
    friends = list(range(1, n + 1))
    start = 0
    while len(friends) > 1:
        out = (start + k - 1) % len(friends)    # jump straight to the k-th friend
        friends.pop(out)                        # the next friend slides into out
        start = out % len(friends)
    return friends[0]

blocks.text: **Time O(n²), space O(n).** The counting is now O(1) per round, but each removal shifts the array: better than the list when k is large, worse when k is small.

Number the seats from 0. With **1** friend the winner is seat 0. Now suppose you know the winner `w` of the game with **i − 1** friends. In the game with **i** friends, the first friend to leave is at seat k − 1, and counting restarts at seat k — so the remaining game is the (i − 1)-friend game with every seat **shifted by k**. The winner with i friends is therefore `(w + k) mod i`.
**Time O(n), space O(1).** No list and no array — just the answer for each smaller circle, built up one friend at a time.

blocks.alt: Circular linked list: O(n·k) time, O(n) space. Array + index math: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Josephus formula: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: In an interview, the circular linked list is the natural first model — it **is** the circle — and shows you can unlink nodes in a ring safely. The formula is the follow-up that shows you can turn a simulation into a recurrence.

items: **k = 1** — friends leave in order 1, 2, 3 … and the last friend, n, wins.
**k larger than n** — counting wraps round the circle more than once; the mod handles it.
**Counting k steps instead of k − 1** — prev must stop on the node **before** the one leaving.
**Elimination Game** — remove every other number, alternating directions: another recurrence on a shrinking line.
**Design Circular Queue** — a fixed-size ring buffer: the same wrap-around idea with array indexes.
**Round-robin scheduling** — an operating system gives each process a turn by walking a circular list of them.
